title: Productivity pain point as inflation, interest rates to hurt until 2028
full_text:
Westpac chief executive Anthony Miller says interest rates could remain elevated into 2028 and “potentially beyond” without any improvement in productivity growth, as new Coalition analysis reveals it could take the Albanese government eight years to regain the productivity levels it inherited in 2022.
Almost a year since Jim Chalmers hosted a three-day economic reform roundtable and pledged to fix the productivity crisis, the chief executives of Australia’s two biggest banks have sounded the alarm about the need to regain historic productivity levels that would push inflation and interest rates down sooner.
Amid private sector fears that the Albanese government, states and territories are struggling to get policy settings right in the battle to lift dire productivity levels, Mr Miller and Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn told The Australian they had bigger concerns about productivity levels than a 5 per cent fall in house prices, which the Reserve Bank said this week would be the consequence of Labor’s tax changes.
Mr Miller, in Canberra on Wednesday to meet Treasury officials and Dr Chalmers, said he thought interest rates could remain high at least into 2028 if there is no improvement in productivity. He linked Labor’s property tax crackdown with a sharp slowdown in housing activity and loan applications.
TAD-2482 Productivity (Part 1)
“We need to recognise one of the reasons (the property tax regime of the 1990s) worked really well in the ’90s, and one of the reasons why we’ve had such a great run as a country, is we were really good on productivity then, we were really focused on productivity,” Mr Miller said.
“I think to ensure that we realise the full benefits and none of the downside from those (tax) reforms we really need to make sure that as a country – whether it be business, labour leaders, government regulators – what we are doing is driving productivity.”
The Treasurer has repeatedly said productivity is a top priority for the government in this term in office but both Treasury and the RBA have downgraded productivity forecasts. Actual productivity levels sank to -0.6 per cent for the March quarter, according to the most recent national accounts.
On Tuesday, the Reserve Bank downgraded its productivity forecasts for the December quarter to -0.5 per cent, down 0.7 percentage points from its previous forecast. Treasury had earlier downgraded its productivity assumption in this year’s budget to 0.7 per cent from 1.2 per cent.
Analysis by the opposition of official figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics reveals that the RBA’s new forecasts indicate the Labor government will not be able to regain the levels of productivity it inherited in 2022 for another eight years, totalling 12.
Angus Taylor said Dr Chalmers’ productivity table last year was a “talkfest” that had only resulted in productivity going “backwards”.
“Now the Reserve Bank says it will take another two years just to get back to an already weak rate of productivity growth,” the Opposition Leader said. “On RBA forecasts it means it will take another eight years to get back to the levels seen before the 2022 election.
TAD-2482 Productivity (Part 2)
“This is the consequence of a government that talks about productivity but taxes investment, piles regulation onto business and grows government faster than the private economy.
“Productivity is ultimately about living standards. When Australians produce more for every hour they work, wages can rise and families can get ahead. Under Labor, productivity has gone backwards and so have living standards.”
Mr Comyn said “we can see that the economy is slowing” and that productivity was more important than a 5 per cent drop in house prices. “I’m not suggesting (house prices) are not an important issue,” he said. “I don’t think it’s as important as longer-term productivity. I think that’s really what underpins the continuous improvements in living standards.
The CBA chief said the economy could not grow beyond about 2 per cent at the moment, without running into inflationary effects.
“So long term, an economy that’s growing at 3 per cent versus 2 per cent because we’re improving productivity is really important,” he said.
HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham said it was hard to gauge how long it would take to get back to the productivity growth levels of the previous decade. “It’s hard to see us getting back to the previous productivity levels over the foreseeable future, it’s hard to see it on the forecast horizon,” he said.
Mr Bloxham said the Covid pandemic had made some of the productivity statistics messy. He noted that between 2005 and 2015 productivity growth averaged 1.3 per cent a year, while between 2016 and 2025 it averaged 0.3 per cent a year. “The RBA has put out a set of forecasts this week that show labour productivity is going to be lower,” he said. “They have lowered their forecasts several times. This means that for the same amount of work done this time last year. Businesses now face high rates and high costs so how will businesses get productivity up? They are either going to have to streamline workforces or take on more AI adoption.”
After Westpac this week revealed investor loan applications had fallen by 30 per cent, Mr Miller said budget hits on negative gearing and capital gains tax discounts had driven uncertainty.
Mr Comyn reported a 28 per cent collapse in investor loan applications since May. The bank, which is the country’s biggest residential lender, also reported a 9 per cent slide in owner occupier lending applications over the same period.
Amid concerns over declining property prices and first homebuyers sliding into negative equity, Mr Miller acknowledged a new reality in which Australians may need to accept home values might not improve “as steep as we’ve seen … in the past”.
